\subsubsection{Converter Readout}\label{sss:pixtop-adc}

The converter's charge-redistribution array exists only in layout, so at
schematic level it makes no bit decisions and the code the assembled channel
reports is not a conversion. The numbers below come from a netlist in which the
extracted converter replaces the schematic one and nothing else changes.

Against known voltages the channel's transfer matches the standalone
characterisation of Section~\ref{ss:adc} to within \SI{3.3}{LSB} across
\SIrange{0.62}{1.87}{\volt}, and three conversions in one run repeat to
\SI{2}{LSB}; on the four levels re-measured through the buffered multiplexer
described below the agreement is \SI{0.4}{LSB}. One LSB is
\SI{1.593}{\milli\volt} over the converter's measured
\SI{1.63}{\volt} span, so what it resolves in current is set by \(R_f\) alone:
\SI{88.5}{\nano\ampere} at \(N = 0\), \SI{4.02}{\nano\ampere} at \(N = 63\) and
\SI{0.825}{\nano\ampere} at \(N = 319\). The zero calibration consequently
cannot be taken at the bottom gain code, where the whole
\SI{34.4}{\nano\ampere} offset is sub-LSB: measured there the code corresponds
to \SI{-73}{\nano\ampere} of apparent current on a \SI{-34}{\nano\ampere}
signal, which is quantisation and not a reading. It must be taken at a
high-gain tap, where one LSB is smaller than the offset being measured --- which
the gain-independent zero of Section~\ref{sss:pixtop-zero} makes free.

\paragraph{The multiplexer no longer disturbs the channel.} A unity-gain buffer
stands between the multiplexer and the converter, so the sample switch draws its
charge from the buffer and the multiplexer drives only a gate. Selecting the
common-mode slot moves that rail by \SI{0.834}{\milli\volt} and the
transimpedance output by \SI{1.75}{\milli\volt} --- \SI{1.1}{LSB} --- both
recovered inside one conversion, the output settling in
\SI{0.54}{\micro\second} to a residual below \SI{1}{\nano\volt}. Without the
buffer the same measurement dragged the common mode \SI{518}{\milli\volt} and
threw the output \SI{1233}{\milli\volt}, with \SI{149}{\milli\volt} still
un-recovered at the end of a \SI{21}{\micro\second} record: it never settled, at
every conversion. \textbf{The gain-independent zero measurement of
Section~\ref{sss:pixtop-zero} is therefore executable on this cell.} The
commanded-potential slot was broken the same way and worse on the residual
(\SI{-99.9}{\milli\volt} at the end of the record) and now peaks at
\SI{0.207}{\milli\volt}; the readout slot is \(51\times\) quieter as a side
effect, its \SI{5.6}{\milli\volt} sampling kick now landing on the buffer's
output where the channel does not see it. Both buffer loops are stable ---
\SI{78.4}{\degree} of phase margin with \SI{17.8}{\decibel} of gain margin at
the converter, \SI{80.9}{\degree} and \SI{20.3}{\decibel} at the test port, and
neither moves with the gain code.

\paragraph{The buffer's offset cancels in the subtraction.} The buffer is the
same amplifier as A2 at the same operating point, so it contributes that
amplifier's own input offset, \SI{-619.6}{\micro\volt}, directly at the
converter input. One buffer downstream of the multiplexer rather than one per
source is what makes this free: every slot is read through it, so the offset
subtracts out of a zero-referenced reading exactly and only its variation with
input level survives. Over 100 Monte Carlo samples that residual is
\SI{0.62}{\milli\volt} mean and \SI{2.07}{\milli\volt} worst across the full
\(\pm\SI{0.8}{\volt}\) readout swing, and \SI{0.031}{\milli\volt} mean,
\SI{0.11}{\milli\volt} worst over \(\pm\SI{150}{\milli\volt}\) --- against a
\SI{5.58}{\milli\volt} \(\sigma\) on the offset itself.

\paragraph{Bit 9 is inverted (firmware-critical).} The raw output bus carries
its most significant bit inverted --- the two's-complement form of the
offset-binary code Section~\ref{ss:adc} describes. Every published converter
number, including the transfer of Table~\ref{tab:adc-transfer}, is the
corrected code \(\mathrm{raw} + 512 - 1024\,b_9\), so firmware must invert bit~9
before using the bus. Read raw, the transfer is a plausible straight line that wraps at the
common-mode code --- a silent 512-code error over half the range.
